title: Photocopy the note that names the task
allegory: A function vector is like an office where, after reading a few worked examples, a handful of clerks write the task ('opposites') on a shared whiteboard; you average that note over many requests so only the task remains, paste a copy onto the board of a request that came with no examples, and the office does the task anyway.
map: the office's shared whiteboard, which every clerk reads and adds to
the few clerks who read the examples and write 'we are doing opposites'
the attention heads with the highest causal indirect effect on the task
averaging the note over many requests, so only the shared task survives
the mean over ICL prompts at the final token: h from the whole stream, or the top heads' summed outputs (the function vector)
pasting a copy onto the board of a request with no examples
adding the vector to a zero-shot prompt's residual stream at the same layer
the model producing antonyms with no demonstrations

cap.1: Show a model pairs like noisy → quiet, then ancient → ?, and it answers with the opposite. It learned the game from examples. Is the game written down inside?
cap.2: That is in-context learning: picking up a task from examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Todd et al. asked whether the task itself exists as a vector.
cap.3: Todd, Li, Sen Sharma, Mueller, Wallace and Bau (ICLR 2024) asked whether 'which task am I doing' is a compact, transportable object in the residual stream.

cap.1: Picture an office with one shared whiteboard. After reading the examples, a few clerks write the game on it: opposites. Everyone after them reads the board.
cap.2: The whiteboard is the residual stream; the clerks are attention heads. At a middle layer, the final token's activation carries the task as well as the words.
cap.3: In GPT-J (28 layers), the layer-12 residual at the final token is where Todd et al. read the task off: averaged over antonym prompts, it gives the vector h.

parts.note: the board at the last token

cap.1: Take the board from many example prompts and average: word details cancel, the game remains. Paste that average into a prompt with no examples.
cap.2: Mean the layer-12 residual stream at the final token over a batch of ICL prompts to get h. Add h at layer 12 of a zero-shot prompt and check the completion.
cap.3: The zero-shot model then produces the antonym it otherwise would not: causal evidence that the stream carries an explicit encoding of the task, not only of the tokens.

cap.1: Which clerks write the note? Scramble the examples so the game is lost, then restore one clerk's work at a time and see who brings the right answer back.
cap.2: Causal indirect effect: patch each head's clean output into a shuffled-label run and measure how much the correct token's probability recovers. Sum the top heads' outputs: that is the function vector.
cap.3: CIE over GPT-J's 28 × 16 = 448 heads gives a (layers, heads) heatmap. The FV is the sum of the selected heads' attn_out contributions, averaged over the dataset.

chapters.name: Slice before the sum
chapters.verdict: Cut the heads apart before out_proj adds them together.

cap.1: The clerks' notes are merged into one before they reach the board. To test one clerk, catch the notes before the merge, not after.
cap.2: In HuggingFace GPT-J, out_proj projects each head and sums them in one matmul. Editing attn_output hits all 16 heads at once, so work on z.
cap.3: Reshape z to (batch, seq, n_heads, d_head), clone, zero all heads but the target, and read out_proj: heads are additive, so that output is exactly the head's contribution.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A task can be a single vector
A handful of heads write it
Paste it in to switch the task on

cap.1: A task taught by example leaves a compact, movable trace inside the model. Find it and you can switch the task on without any examples.
cap.2: The same recipe on country-capital pairs steers free generation: 'When you think of Netherlands, you usually think of' continues with Amsterdam.
cap.3: For understanding and steering AI: function vectors change what the model computes, steering vectors change how it sounds, and both are found by forward passes, not training.

coda.title: One prompt's activation is the task plus word clutter: average more prompts

readouts.label: match with the shared task direction (cosine)

caption.1: Each bar is one direction of an activation. One prompt mixes the task with clutter from its words. Average more prompts and watch the clutter cancel.
caption.2: This is how h is built: the mean final-token activation over many ICL prompts. The shared part survives averaging; prompt-specific parts shrink. Toy numbers, real recipe.
caption.3: Mean of n samples of t + ε: ε shrinks roughly as 1/√n, t is untouched. Anything all prompts share survives, format included; the head-based FV narrows h to what the task heads write.

where_else: Steering vectors, the sibling trick: built from contrasting prompt pairs to change how the model sounds
Activation patching and the IOI circuit work, which use the same causal-effect machinery to find the heads that matter
The Assistant axis in [4.4]: a persona found as a direction you can push along or cap

hamming.what: A single vector, averaged from a model's activations on prompts that demonstrate a task by example, that makes the model perform the task on a bare prompt when added in.
hamming.when: When you want to find where a model keeps the task it inferred from examples, or to switch that task on without giving any examples.
hamming.why: It shows the task is a compact, movable object written by a handful of attention heads, not something diffused across the whole context.

object.title: The task shift
object.subtitle: A schematic of activation space: prompts with antonym examples, bare prompts, and the same bare prompts after the function vector is added.

cap.1: Each dot is one prompt's state at a middle layer, final token. Prompts with antonym examples sit together; bare prompts sit elsewhere.
cap.2: Schematic: the real residual stream has far more dimensions; three stand in for them here.
cap.3: Final-token residual activations at layer 12 over an ICL dataset; averaging them, or the top heads' outputs, gives the task vector.

cap.1: Average the example prompts and the word details cancel. What they all share is the task.
cap.2: h is the batch mean of the layer-12 residual at the final token over antonym ICL prompts.
cap.3: Averaging keeps every shared component; the head-based FV narrows h to what a handful of high-CIE heads write.

cap.1: Add the vector to the bare prompts and they shift along the task direction. Now they answer with antonyms, with no examples.
cap.2: Add the FV to the zero-shot prompt's residual stream at the same layer, then read the completion.
cap.3: An intervention on the zero-shot forward pass: the paper's evidence that the task is an explicit, transportable object in the stream.

cap.1: Same recipe, another task: a country-capital vector makes 'When you think of Netherlands, you usually think of' continue with Amsterdam.
cap.2: ARENA steers multi-token generation with a vector from a held-out country-capital task.
cap.3: With .generate() and a KV cache, intervene once per generated token via model.next(), unless the addition is fixed on the prompt positions, which the cache carries forward.

cap.1: Unlike a steering vector, nobody chose a contrast here. The model's own examples wrote this vector.
cap.2: Function vectors come from attention-head outputs on ICL tasks; steering vectors come from contrastive prompt pairs.
cap.3: Both are found by forward passes rather than gradient descent: function vectors change what the model computes, steering vectors how it sounds.

predict.q: You add h to a bare prompt with no examples. What does the model do?

options.t: Nothing: without examples the task is gone

predict.why: That is the paper's first result: the task travels inside the vector, so the examples are no longer needed.

predict.q: You edit attn_output to knock out one head. What actually happens?

options.t: All 16 heads in the layer are hit, because out_proj already summed them

predict.why: In HuggingFace GPT-J, out_proj projects and sums the heads in one matmul. Edit z, before out_proj, where the heads are still separate.

predict.q: How do you find which heads carry the task?

options.t: Patch each head's clean output into shuffled-label runs and see which restores the answer
Pick the heads with the largest outputs

predict.why: Causal indirect effect measures what a head does for the task, not how loud it is.
